result.summary: Pausanias traces the Arcadian kings from Echemus down to the second Aristocrates, tying them to the Dorian return, the Trojan War, Cyprus and the Messenian wars. The line ends when the Arcadians stone two kings for impiety and treachery and depose the descendants of Cypselus.

scenes.title: Echemus and the Dorian invasion
scenes.summary: Echemus becomes king and kills Hyllus in single combat. Agapenor then succeeds him and leads the Arcadians to Troy.
scenes.stakes: The Arcadians face the Dorian invasion of the Peloponnese.

scenes.title: Agapenor founds Paphos
scenes.summary: A storm drives Agapenor to Cyprus, where he founds Paphos and its temple of Aphrodite. His daughter Laodice later sends a robe to Tegea.
scenes.stakes: Agapenor's fleet is endangered by the storm and he cannot return home.

scenes.title: Kings from Hippothous to Simus
scenes.summary: The throne passes through Hippothous, Æpytus, Cypselus, Olæas, Bucolion, Phialus and Simus. Æpytus is struck blind for entering Poseidon's temple, and the Dorians return.
scenes.stakes: Arcadia must avoid conquest by the returning Dorians; Æpytus risks divine wrath.

scenes.title: Pompus to Æchmis
scenes.summary: Pompus befriends the Æginetans, and later kings see Tegea defeat Charillus and the Arcadians side with the Messenians against Sparta.
scenes.stakes: Arcadia is drawn into war between Sparta and Messenia.

scenes.title: Fall of the house of Cypselus
scenes.summary: Aristocrates violates Artemis's priestess at her altar and is stoned. His grandson of the same name takes Spartan bribes and betrays the Messenians, and is also stoned, ending the dynasty.
scenes.stakes: Aristocrates risks death at the Arcadians' hands for impiety and treachery.

alias_notes.explanation: Cult title of Artemis at her temple between Orchomenus and Mantinea.

notable_quotes.reason: Quoted inscription on Laodice's robe, linking Cyprus to Tegea.

analysis.text: The chapter is a king list that links Arcadia to wider Greek events and shows divine punishment of impious acts.
Pausanias reconciles genealogies with the Dorian return and Messenian wars, and revises his own earlier account.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias openly corrects his earlier account of when Orestes reigned.

language_notes.text: The Dorians' return under Hyllus, son of Hercules, is the 'Return of the Heraclidae', the legendary Dorian conquest of the Peloponnese.
Pausanias refers back to his own earlier account, in which he named Orestes as Achaean king at the time.
The storm refers to the tempests that scattered the Greek fleets returning from Troy (Ilium).
'Gives the nationality' means the inscription shows Laodice was from Cyprus, as 'sacred Cyprus' indicates.
'Three generations earlier' points back to Hyllus's failed attempt by the Isthmus; this return is by sea near Rhium.
'In junction with' means 'jointly with'; the Heraclidae are the descendants of Hercules.
Cyllene was the port of Elis on the western coast; the Æginetans landed goods there and carried them inland.
"Out of friendship to them" means Pompus named his son Æginetes, 'the Æginetan', as a compliment to the traders.
Refers to the First Messenian War against Sparta; Aristodemus was the Messenian king in the later Messenian wars Pausanias describes elsewhere.
"Defiled her" is a euphemism for rape; seeking refuge at an altar was meant to protect a suppliant.
Means the priestess was henceforth an older woman who had given up relations with men, not a young maiden.
The Great Trench was the site of a decisive Messenian defeat, where Arcadian king Aristocrates is said to have betrayed his allies.

context_notes.text: Paphos on Cyprus became the famous cult centre of Aphrodite, said to have risen from the sea near the island.
Athene Alea was the chief goddess of Tegea, with a celebrated temple there.
Poseidon's temple at Mantinea was forbidden to all; entering it was sacrilege, and Pausanias records the punishment.
Black Demeter was a Phigalian cult image of the grain goddess, shown dark in mourning for her lost daughter.
Charillus was a Spartan king. The Tegean women's role in defeating him is a local tradition Pausanias promises to expand on.
Artemis Hymnia was an Arcadian cult title of the goddess; her sanctuary lay between Orchomenus and Mantinea.
Stoning was a communal punishment, showing the Arcadians treated the crime as one against the whole people and the goddess.

literary_notes.text: Æpytus, seeking to see the forbidden shrine, loses his sight; the punishment fits the transgression.
The burning of the sacred statue is presented as an omen of the king's coming death.
Pausanias speaks in the first person, stressing his duty as a historian to record the king's impiety.
The grandson repeats his grandfather's name and fate, framing the dynasty's treachery as a pattern of crime and punishment.
The closing statement gives the dynasty's fall a moral cause, completing the arc begun by the first Aristocrates' impiety.
